name: South Slopes via Emerald-Saska Col

approach_variants.name: North Fork Entiat and the primitive Pyramid Creek Trail to the Emerald-Saska basin
camps: The basin between Emerald and Saska, and Milham Pass
Cottonwood Camp and the Entiat River road campgrounds
Fox Camp, North Fork Entiat trail
approach_variants.notes: From the North Fork Entiat Trailhead near 3,880-3,940 ft at the end of FR-5606, the first four miles of Trail #1437 climb gently up the valley through old burn, where blowdown and washed-out sections make the going slower than the grade suggests. There is little shade and the valley bottom runs hot and dry — carry water. Continue up-valley another four miles, gaining roughly 3,000 ft from the trailhead, to the Pyramid Creek / Fern Lake junction. That junction is anywhere from seven to nine miles in depending on how far up the road you were able to start. Fox Camp sits about a quarter mile north of it. From the junction take the primitive, unmaintained Pyramid Creek Trail west and climb about 1,000 ft over a mile to a mile and a half into the upper basin between Emerald and Saska, around 7,100 ft. The tread is intermittent. Pushing to that camp rather than stopping at the junction costs an extra hour on the approach day and returns about the same on summit day. This is reported as the easiest and shortest of the Saska / Emerald / Cardinal trio's summit scrambles.
approach_variants.season: Mid-Jul-Sep once the col and summit gullies clear. October adds larch colour and early-snow risk; before mid-July carry an axe for lingering snow and ice
hazards: Loose rock and rockfall throughout the Emerald-Saska col basin and along the summit ridge
Cliff bands below the south-west face that have caught descending parties in icy or snow-covered conditions
A narrow, sometimes knife-edged connecting crest that has to be avoided rather than followed
Lingering snow and ice in the col and summit gullies into early-to-mid July in heavy years
Heavy blowdown and washed-out sections on the lower North Fork Entiat Trail from past wildfires and storm damage
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base is the col and the direction off it is west. From the basin camp, about 600 ft of gain on talus, scree or lingering snow reaches the Emerald-Saska Col at roughly 7,700 ft — a notch on the south ridge with a peak on either side. From the col, head west toward Saska. Emerald is the other way. If you leave the col climbing east you are on the neighbouring peak's ground.

The positive test is that you do not stay on the crest. The connecting ridge is narrow and knife-edged in places with steep drop-offs on both sides, so the usual line drops slightly onto its west flank to pick up an obvious scree-and-rock gully, then follows a cairned rising traverse back toward the crest. West flank, gully, cairned rising traverse. A party grimly balancing along the crest itself has missed the line rather than found the hard way.

The finish is counted in feet, not features: roughly 300 ft of final Class 3 on loose blocks gains the top. Test every hold — nothing here is fixed and no rope is standard, although the last exposed moves are steep enough that some parties carry a short handline for them.

The descent marker is a warning with a documented consequence: cliff bands sit below the south-west face. Stay well clear of them when the ground is snow-covered or icy. A winter party misjudging that descent line in icy conditions lost a ski over those cliffs. In early-to-mid season the continuous snow below the col gives a glissade or boot-ski; by August and September the same ground is loose scree and dirt that has to be walked slowly.

Loose rock is the theme of the whole cirque. Helmet, and do not stack the party directly above one another, from the moment you leave the basin.

approach_variants.name: Lake Chelan: Lucerne and Emerald Park to Milham Pass

bivy.name: The basin between Emerald and Saska, and Milham Pass
bivy.notes: The high camp for the crest traverse, about a mile and a half beyond Fox Camp on the Pyramid trail, in the basin that separates Emerald Peak from Saska Peak. This is where a party stages to link Cardinal, Emerald, Saska and Pinnacle Mountain in a single push over Milham Pass at about 6,663 ft, which is the classic way to do these four and much the most efficient. From the basin you climb to the upper shelf just below the ridge between Emerald and Saska and pick up the broad gully to the summit. Cardinal is the highest of the group and the furthest, and it is the one that turns a two-day plan into three. The setting is superb and the ground is loose — expect scree and blocky scrambling rather than clean rock, and expect the descents to take longer than the ascents. Season is short at this height in a heavy year, realistically mid-July to early October, and the reason to come late is the larch and the reason not to is the water. Weigh that honestly: an August party that finds the tarns dry has a long, hot walk back down to fix it. Weather moves in from the west with little warning here and the basin is fully exposed.
bivy.water: Snowmelt tarns and rivulets in the basin, and these are the crux of the whole plan. They are dependable in early and mid summer, unreliable by mid-August, and in a dry year they are gone entirely by late August, at which point the nearest certain water is back down at Fox Camp. Do not commit to a high camp here in late season without either confirming water or carrying it up. Milham Pass itself has none.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue, party limit of twelve. Camp on durable ground and well back from the tarns. No campfires — forest-wide restrictions aside, there is no fuel at this elevation and the ground is fragile. Reached only through trails inside the Little Giant Fire closure area (Okanogan-Wenatchee order 06-17-07-2026-40), in effect September 3 through October 31, 2026 unless lifted sooner.
bivy.capacity: A small number of tent-sized spots on benches and moraine in the upper basin; two or three parties at most, and less if you want flat ground

approach_variants.notes: Take the boat up Lake Chelan to Lucerne, then climb the trail past the Domke Lake junction and up Emerald Park Creek to Emerald Park, about 6.5 miles, and on another two miles to Milham Pass. Drop from the pass into the basin between Emerald and Saska and pick up the south-slopes route there. A long, remote approach that suits parties already on the Lake Chelan side.

road.name: Entiat River Road (County Road 19 → Forest Road 51) to Forest Road 5606
road.status: Paved for roughly the first 27 miles from the town of Entiat, then gravel Forest Road 51 to the FR 5606 junction at about 32.3 miles, then gravel FR 5606 north for a final 3 miles to the trailhead (~35.3 miles total); subject to intermittent washout/landslide damage. Closed: the Little Giant Fire closure (Okanogan-Wenatchee order 06-17-07-2026-40, in effect since September 3, 2026 and through October 31, 2026 unless lifted sooner) closes FR 5606 and the North Fork Entiat River Trail #1437. Check with the Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest before you go.
road.driveNote: From US-97A in Entiat, follow Entiat River Road/Forest Road 51 about 32.3 miles, then turn right (north) onto Forest Road 5606 for a final 3 miles to its end at the North Fork Entiat Trailhead (el. ~3,940 ft), about 35.3 miles total. Expect washboard gravel and creek-crossing damage on the upper miles; high-clearance recommended, and a trailer ban may be in effect if a slide bypass is active — verify current status before driving up.

approach: Standard access is the North Fork Entiat River Trail (#1437) from the North Fork Entiat Trailhead (el. ~3,940 ft, at the end of Forest Road 5606, about 35.3 mi from the town of Entiat via Entiat River Road/Forest Road 51 then FR 5606). The trail crosses old fire-damaged forest with blowdown for its first miles, enters Glacier Peak Wilderness at about mile 4 (free self-issue permit required at the boundary), and reaches the Pyramid Creek/Fern Lake trail junction roughly 7-9 miles in depending on trip reports and current trailhead access (road washouts have periodically forced parties to start several miles below the official trailhead — check current Forest Service alerts). From the junction, the primitive, unmaintained Pyramid Creek Trail climbs west about 1,000 ft over roughly 1-1.5 miles into the high basin between Emerald and Saska; most parties camp either at Fox Camp near the junction or push on to a larch-meadow camp directly beneath the Emerald-Saska col for a shorter summit day.

waypoints.name: North Fork Entiat River Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of FR 5606, about 35.3 mi from Entiat (32.3 mi on Entiat River Road/FR 51 + 3 mi on FR 5606); start of North Fork Entiat River Trail #1437, Northwest Forest Pass required with self-issue wilderness permit at the kiosk.
waypoints.directions: From US 97A at Entiat, turn onto Entiat River Road (County Road 19, which becomes FR 51) and drive 32.3 miles to FR 5606; if you reach North Fork Campground you have gone too far. Follow FR 5606 for 3 miles to the road end at about 3,900 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park, and a free Glacier Peak Wilderness permit is self-issued at the kiosk.

waypoints.name: Glacier Peak Wilderness Boundary
waypoints.note: Trail crosses into Glacier Peak Wilderness here; stock/group-size rules apply beyond this point, no additional permit needed.
waypoints.directions: The first four miles of the North Fork Entiat River Trail #1437 climb gently up the valley through old burn, where blowdown and washed-out sections make the going slower than the grade suggests. There is little shade on this stretch and the east-side valley bottom runs hot and dry in summer — carry more water than the mileage implies.

waypoints.name: Fox Camp (Pyramid Creek Trail junction)
waypoints.note: Established camp just off the North Fork Entiat trail where the Pyramid Creek Trail forks west; standard base camp for Saska/Emerald/Cardinal objectives.
waypoints.directions: Continue up the North Fork Entiat valley another four miles, gaining roughly 3,000 ft from the trailhead to the Pyramid Creek / Fern Lake junction; the camp itself sits about a quarter mile north of the junction. This junction is anywhere from seven to nine miles in depending on how far up the road you were able to start, so navigate by the drainage and the fork rather than by an odometer.

waypoints.name: Basin between Emerald and Saska
waypoints.note: 1.5 mi up the Pyramid Creek Trail from Fox Camp into the upper basin below Emerald and Saska; talus/snow camping, last reliable water before the col.
waypoints.directions: From the junction take the primitive Pyramid Creek Trail west and climb steadily for roughly a mile and a half into the upper basin. The tread is unmaintained and intermittent. Pushing to this camp instead of stopping at the junction costs an extra hour on the approach day and takes about that much off the summit morning.

waypoints.name: Emerald-Saska col saddle
waypoints.note: Climb scree/talus (snow-filled gully early season) out of the basin to the notch on the ridge connecting Emerald and Saska; route splits toward either summit here.
waypoints.directions: Roughly 600 ft of gain out of the basin to the notch. Loose rock is the theme of this whole cirque — wear a helmet and avoid stacking the party directly above one another. In early-to-mid season continuous snow on this slope allows a glissade or boot-ski on the way back down; by August and September that is gone and the same ground becomes slow, controlled scree steps rather than good scree-skiing.

waypoints.name: Summit scree/talus gully
waypoints.note: Loose scree gully with Class 3 rock bands above the col; exposed and rockfall-prone, especially with other parties above on the south slopes.
waypoints.directions: Head west from the col toward Saska. The connecting crest is narrow and knife-edged in places with steep drop-offs on both sides, so the usual line drops slightly onto its west flank to pick up an obvious scree-and-rock gully, then follows a cairned rising traverse back toward the crest. Everything underfoot moves — keep the party close together and out of each other's fall line.

waypoints.name: Saska Peak
waypoints.note: True summit of Saska Peak (8,404 ft); broad views of Emerald and Cardinal Peaks and the North Fork Entiat headwaters.
waypoints.directions: Roughly 300 ft of final class 3 scrambling on loose blocks gains the top. Test every hold: nothing is fixed and no rope is standard here, though the last exposed moves are steep enough that some parties carry a short handline for them. This is the stretch that punishes a late finish or poor visibility on the way back down, so set your turnaround before you leave the col.
